reference.source: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology / Fitzpatrick's Dermatology
clinicalPearls: Presents with hyperpigmented, slightly verrucous or scaly papules that coalesce centrally into confluent plaques and form a reticulate (net-like) pattern at the periphery
Characteristically involves the upper trunk (central chest, upper back, and the intermammary and interscapular regions), sometimes extending to the neck and axillae
Typically affects adolescents and young adults and is usually asymptomatic or only mildly itchy
Frequently confused with acanthosis nigricans (which is velvety and flexural) and with pityriasis versicolor
The actinomycete Dietzia papillomatosis and, historically, the yeast Malassezia have been implicated, and many patients respond dramatically to oral minocycline
Best understood as a disorder of keratinisation with an abnormal host response to microbial colonisation
Potassium hydroxide microscopy is typically negative or shows only incidental Malassezia, helping to distinguish it from pityriasis versicolor
First-line treatment is oral minocycline (or an alternative tetracycline or macrolide), with topical retinoids, keratolytics, and antifungals as adjuncts
reference.pathophysiology: Confluent and reticulated papillomatosis is best understood as a disturbance of epidermal keratinisation. The leading hypotheses invoke an aberrant cutaneous reaction to microbial colonisation, with the actinomycete Dietzia papillomatosis and the commensal yeast Malassezia both proposed as triggers, while a subset of cases is linked to endocrine and metabolic factors such as insulin resistance and obesity. Whatever the initiating factor, the epidermis responds with papillomatosis, hyperkeratosis, and increased basal pigmentation, producing the confluent central plaques and reticulate peripheral pattern. The frequently rapid response to minocycline supports a microbial or anti-inflammatory contribution to the mechanism.
additionalInvestigations: Potassium hydroxide microscopy of scale to exclude pityriasis versicolor
Skin biopsy showing papillomatosis, hyperkeratosis, and increased basal-layer pigmentation
A trial of oral minocycline as a supportive diagnostic and therapeutic measure
Screening for insulin resistance and the metabolic syndrome in appropriate patients
Wood's lamp examination to help exclude the fluorescence of pityriasis versicolor
redFlags: Failure to respond to antimicrobial therapy, prompting reconsideration of acanthosis nigricans and its causes
Features suggesting underlying insulin resistance or an endocrinopathy
Rapidly extensive velvety change raising the possibility of malignant acanthosis nigricans when the diagnosis is in doubt
reference.prognosis: Benign and largely cosmetic in impact; it usually responds well to minocycline with clearance over weeks, although relapses can occur and maintenance or repeat courses may be required.
pitfalls: Diagnosing pityriasis versicolor and repeatedly treating with antifungals without response
Not distinguishing it from acanthosis nigricans, which points to a different underlying workup
Overlooking the typically excellent response to minocycline
Attributing a negative potassium hydroxide result to sampling error rather than reconsidering the diagnosis
management: Treat first-line with oral minocycline, which frequently produces rapid clearance; other tetracyclines such as doxycycline are alternatives
Consider other oral antibiotics such as a macrolide (azithromycin or clarithromycin) where tetracyclines are unsuitable
Use topical or oral retinoids, or topical vitamin D analogues and keratolytics, as options in resistant disease given the underlying disorder of keratinisation
Screen for and address insulin resistance, obesity and the metabolic syndrome in appropriate patients
Reassure the patient regarding the benign, largely cosmetic nature of the condition
Anticipate relapse and provide maintenance or repeat courses of treatment as required
